book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

chapters.file: ch05 - Who’s Putting Ideas in Your Head.md
chapters.relation: The book's introduction frames Inception around two threats to the self: the old Cartesian doubt that we can never be sure we are not dreaming, and a newer neuroscience-based worry that even our thoughts are not our own because we act on them before we become aware of them. It surveys the volume's guiding questions - whether inception, unlike the implants of Blade Runner and Dark City, is a wrong akin to propaganda, advertising or brainwashing; whether Second Life-style virtual worlds mean walking away from reality; and whether even 'true inspiration' can be faked. It also previews the book's boldest readings, such as the theory that the whole film is Cobb's single dream on the flight and the claim that the dreams run on a server, making Mal into 'Mal-ware'.

chapters.file: ch06 - Level 1 - Come Back to Reality, Please.md

chapters.relation: Wenmackers uses Inception's dream levels and its ambiguous spinning-top ending as a guided tour of skeptical philosophy, diagramming how dreams-within-dreams, kicks, Limbo and exponentially dilated dream time work. She tests the totem against Zhuangzi's butterfly and lucid-dreaming reality checks, then runs Plato's Cave and the eternal Forms, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine to ask whether Cobb's world - or ours - is real. Her conclusion is Socratic ('know that you know nothing'): subjective reality feels equally real on every level and the top level can never be known. She even argues that dream-time dilation means Cobb should not kill himself while in doubt, since real time barely passes, so a little philosophy rescues the happy ending.

chapters.file: ch08 - Legal and Not So Legal Forms of Inception.md
chapters.relation: Brogaard argues Inception's dream technology is closer to real neuroscience than it looks: against Hobson's activation-synthesis model (with Dennett's picture of dreams as narratives concocted on waking) she cites Foulkes, Antrobus and Solms to locate dreaming in dopamine-driven frontal motivation areas, so the film's streamlined plot-driven shared dreams cannot be ruled out. LaBerge's lucid-dream mask shows dream content can be manipulated, split-brain research plus transcranial magnetic stimulation suggests how one mind could tap another's right hemisphere, and the 'embedded dreams' are best read as a single dream whose deeper layers surface as the subject's own beliefs let his guard down. She closes with the legal and illegal inception we already practice: salesmen's mind games and fear conditioning via a temporarily deactivated hippocampus.

chapters.file: ch09 - Does the Top Fall Does It Matter in the End.md
chapters.relation: Andersen contends Inception goes one deeper than Descartes: where the dream argument threatened only the external world, inception threatens the autonomy of thought itself, since the 'core conception' that defines identity - Fischer's reading of his father's dying word 'disappointed' - can be implanted. Tracing Nolan's obsession with thought-manipulation through his earlier films (the manipulator Cobb of Following, Leonard's self-deception in Memento, the Joker's schemes), he shows inception as co-opting subjectivity. Against the Cartesian answer of doubting everything, the fates of Mal and Cobb in Limbo - where doubt, once planted, grows devastatingly, and where a totem cannot guard against self-deception - teach that the way back to reality is the leap of trust in others: only by opening himself to Ariadne, Miles and his children can Cobb turn away from the top and go home.

Rennett tests Cobb's choice to leave Limbo against Nozick's three reasons for refusing the experience machine: we want to actually do things (raise his real children, not loving projections), to be a certain kind of person (Yusuf's dream-den addicts are 'indeterminate blobs'), and to touch something deeper than a man-made world. He then recruits Berkeley's esse est percipi to explain Mal's sincerity - she perceives Limbo and remembers it, so for her it is real - and argues that shared dreams differ from private dreams and the experience machine because they leave waking traces, like Mal's bullet in Arthur's leg. The chapter ends by making reality a matter of choice: like the cave prisoners of Plato's allegory, each character believes a world, and Cobb's ignoring of the top is his choice to live in the world with his children.

chapters.file: ch11 - Level 2 - We’re Not in Your Dream.md

chapters.relation: Testerman turns inception against itself: Cobb and Saito believe they freely plan the Fischer job, but conscious will is a feeling, not a cause. From William James's effortful attention and Dewey's willpower she moves to Penfield's stimulated patients and Libet's readiness-potential experiments showing the brain prepares action before we feel we will it, so Fischer, Cobb and Saito are all equally 'incepted' by subconscious forces - 'freedom is ignorance of the causes of actions', as she glosses Spinoza, with Hume's point that causality is only inferred. Advertising, the foot-in-the-door effect and subliminal primes already do inception's work more cheaply, and the team's 'group will' flows from Saito's own unexamined drive for power, so against Socrates she concludes the unexamined life is perfectly suitable for living.

Malloy argues the real protagonists of Inception are corporations: Cobol Engineering, Proclus Global and Fischer-Morrow move Cobb, Saito and Fischer like chess pieces, making the film a case study in corporate moral personhood. He builds personhood from the capacity to contract and hold rights (Saito buying the airline as Proclus's representative), to bear responsibility for what is done in its name, and to decide through corporate procedures, and he rebuts the objections that corporations lack moral emotions and virtues or vices by distinguishing personhood from personality - psychopaths are still moral persons. He ends with Fischer-Morrow's dilemma between Friedman's shareholder-primacy view and the duties of a member of a moral community, concluding that a monopoly on half the world's energy supply would wrong that community.

Schulzke argues inception's fundamental wrongness is a violation of autonomy read through Kant: the Fischer team treats him merely as a means, and even Cobb's benevolently intended inception on Mal disrespects humanity by stripping her self-determination, leaving her - like someone acting under coercion - no longer a responsible moral agent. Extraction he judges the lesser evil, though a world of dream espionage would end private mental life, since even the most guarded secrets surface in dreams. The payoff is a new twist on the Ring of Gyges from Plato's Republic: an invisibility ring could no longer shield injustice because a dreamer's deeds remain recorded and extractable, so Kant's absolute ban on lying could make extraction an engine of honesty - as when Ariadne's extraction on Cobb exposes the danger Mal poses and ultimately saves Cobb himself.

Garvin asks whether anything done in a dream can be right or wrong, arguing that the dream-share changes the stakes: lies told inside Fischer's shared dream deceive a real dreamer, so ordinary moral rules carry over even when violence targets 'just projections'. The hard case is that projections are indistinguishable from fellow dreamers - his Turing-test argument that either you cannot know whom you are shooting, or a projection as convincing, independent and communicative as a person deserves the same moral standing. For ordinary unshared dreams he parts ways with Augustine on dream-lust: the sleeping self that neither knows nor controls what it does is not responsible for it, though the partial control of lucid dreaming would reopen dream actions to moral judgment.

chapters.file: ch17 - Do We Give Shakespeare the Last Word.md
chapters.relation: Kapper reads Inception as epistemology rather than metaphysics - not what is real but how we could know - running from Plato's Theaetetus (the first dream-recognition question) through Descartes's deceptive demon and Freud's royal road to the unconscious, to Wittgenstein's point that 'I may be dreaming' is senseless because the remark itself would be dreamed, and Heraclitus's line that only the waking share a common world. The Ariadne thread is the clue: as in the Theseus myth, dream architecture gives the labyrinth a shareable narrative place, but only a hint, never a way to wake. He then goes east - Zhuangzi's butterfly, Indra's net of mutually reflecting jewels, Schopenhauer's universe dreamed by a single dreamer, William James's many consciousnesses - to ask how many times we must die before waking, ending with Buddhism: 'Buddha means awakened one', and Cobb's turning from the top enacts Nirvana, where the real-versus-dream question stops pertaining.

Auxier sets out to explain how Fischer could be trained to 'militarize' his subconscious, and to resolve the plot's loose ends: why the snow fortress is really Eames's dream, why Eames plants the pinwheel in the safe, and what Fischer actually knows at baggage claim. The engine is Susanne Langer's theory of mythic consciousness - dreams become communicable only when narrativized, so lucid group dreaming sits between private dream and story, and inception succeeds when a symbol (the pinwheel) is transformed as it spreads until its source is untraceable and Fischer believes he placed it himself. Moderns, he concludes, are easy to incept with doubt - which is what Cobb did to Mal and what Nolan does to us in the theater - and the chapter closes by training readers to resist planting doubts in the people around them.

Dionne argues Cobb's 'most resilient parasite' works only as an idea embedded in a coherent story - 'my father doesn't want me to be him' - and that since ideas define who we are, each person is less a host than a collection of well-planted narratives. Using Bergson on embodied, memory-and-desire-mediated perception (Cobb's fear of the bridge triggering Mal's projection) and Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil on perspectival appearance as the price of life, she claims dreams differ from reality in degree, not kind: we are beings-in-the-world who stabilize contingency through story-making and 'strive for positive logic'. Hence knowledge always demands the leap of faith that Saito and Mal demand of Cobb, the film becomes a meta-narrative with Fischer as its audience, and the wobbling top offers only an interpretation of a fact, never the fact itself.

holes.name: Corporate Moral Personhood
holes.what: The question whether a corporation can be a bearer of moral rights and responsibilities - a moral person or agent - beyond its status as a legal fiction.
holes.why: Chapter 13's entire argument is that Cobol, Proclus Global and Fischer-Morrow are moral persons because they have interests, rights, responsibilities and decision procedures, and no taxonomy slug covers corporate personhood or business ethics.

holes.name: Milton Friedman
holes.what: Twentieth-century economist who argued that a corporation's only social responsibility is to maximize profits for its stockholders within the rules of the game.
holes.why: Chapter 13 stages whether Fischer-Morrow must break itself up as a choice between Friedman's shareholder-primacy doctrine and the view that a corporation owes duties to the moral community.

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis who treated dreams as the 'royal road to the unconscious', where forbidden wishes surface in disguised symbolic form, held back by the ego's censorship.
holes.why: Chapters 8, 17 and 18 all lean on Freud's unconscious-and-ego model of dreaming - as Hobson's foil, as the royal road that inception exploits, and as the sentinel that implanted symbols must sneak past - and taxonomy.json has no psychoanalysis entry.

holes.name: Susanne Langer
holes.what: Philosopher of symbolism whose Philosophy in a New Key explains mythic consciousness: dreams become communicable myth only when transformed into narrative form.
holes.why: Chapter 18's account of dream architecture, lucid group dreaming and inception as untraceable symbol-transformation is explicitly built on Langer's theory.
